title: two Error classes in one Action's failure channel that mint one durable failure identity are refused, and the diagnostic names both classes

diagnostics.messageContains: Error classes Failed and Failed in this Action's declared failure channel share one durable failure identity

xfail.reason: The fork reports the SMITHERS4124 this case declares at the identical code, line, column and sentence — measured, not assumed — and ALSO reports SMITHERS1150@15:32 ('duplicate Error class name 'Failed' cannot receive a stable module-local identity'), which the reference does not report on this program. The judge compares full diagnostic lists, so [SMITHERS1150, SMITHERS4124] cannot satisfy [SMITHERS4124] and the marker is the only way to declare SMITHERS4124 at all. The marker holds NO fail-open: the fork refuses this program, it does not accept it, so the observation is `diagnostics` rather than `output` and this case cannot appear under 'Markers holding a fail-open'. THE DIVERGENCE IS ABOUT SMITHERS1150, NOT ABOUT SMITHERS4124, and it is pre-existing: both implementations own a rule refusing two nominal Error classes that share one name in one module, and they disagree about whether a class declared inside a `namespace` is in that module for its purposes. The fork says yes; the reference says no. Neither answer is obviously wrong and the question belongs to the nominal-error area, not the durable one. THIS CASE COULD NOT AVOID IT. The durable failure identity became INJECTIVE over distinct class names on 2026-08-28 — which is why the corpus's older collision case was renamed `two-error-classes-whose-durable-identities-used-to-collide-now-compile` and is an acceptance today — so the only programs that still reach SMITHERS4124 are ones holding two classes that genuinely have the SAME name in the same file, and a same-name pair in one file is exactly the input SMITHERS1150 exists to refuse. Cross-module spellings do not work either: the identity is minted per source file, so two classes named `Failed` in two modules get two identities and never collide. The set of programs that reach this rule and do not also reach SMITHERS1150 therefore appears to be empty, which makes the marker a property of the rule's reachability rather than of this case's drafting. IF the nominal-error lanes settle whether a namespaced declaration is module-local, one backend moves and this marker retires with a one-line edit to the declared list; nothing about the durable rule changes either way.
xfail.doc: specification/durable-execution.mdx §Durable Boundary Contract requires every value crossing a persistence boundary to satisfy the compiler-checked durable codec contract, which is what makes a non-injective failure identity a compile error rather than a replay hazard. No sentence in specification/failures.mdx or specification/type-system.mdx states whether an Error class declared inside a `namespace` is 'in one module' for the purposes of the module-local nominal identity rule. That silence is the gap this marker cites, and it is a documentation conflict rather than an implementation defect.

notes: WHAT THE RULE IS: a durable failure identity is the string a persisted Action failure is recorded under, so a replay can decide which Error class to rebuild from storage. Two classes sharing one identity make that decision unanswerable — the executor reads one identity and has two constructors to choose between, and would have to pick by declaration order, which is precisely the kind of order dependence the durable boundary exists to remove. WHY THIS CASE EXISTS: SMITHERS4124 is enforced by both implementations and was declared by nothing. Its original case, `17-durable/two-error-classes-whose-durable-identities-used-to-collide-now-compile`, turned over from a refusal into an ACCEPTANCE when the identity became injective on 2026-08-28, and the declaration left with the verdict. That is the same shape as this revision's other two durable cases but arrived at differently: 4111 and 4112 lost their declarations to step 11's wall withdrawal, and 4124 lost its to a repair that made the old program legal. In all three the rule stayed in both backends with nothing declaring it. RE-DERIVED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: the program here is NOT the one the deleted case used. The `$Failed`/`_Failed` pair that case held compiles today. What still collides is two classes with a genuinely identical name, and a `namespace` is the smallest legal spelling of that in authored `.sm` — and unlike the old pair, no better algorithm can take it away, which is why the diagnostic names one class twice ('Error classes Failed and Failed'): the two declarations really do have the same name. WHY messageContains: a code and a position alone are satisfied by any refusal at that call, including the generic 'higher-order and dynamic calls are unavailable in durable source lowering' that this program used to draw before SMITHERS4124 was minted for it. That sentence is FALSE of this program — `Pick.run({ key: input.key })` is an ordinary compiler-bound Action call with no higher-order or dynamic call anywhere in the file — and it sent authors hunting for a call that is not there. The naming of both classes is the whole repair, so the fragment holds it. THE DECLARED POSITION: 20:10 is the `Pick.run(...)` call site, not the class declarations. Both implementations anchor here deliberately: the collision is discovered while deriving the Action's contract but re-reported at each caller, because the caller is where the author can act on it.
